verses.translation: And he showed{H7200} me one{H259} wadi{H5158} that was full{H4392} of living{H2416} waters{H4325}, and clear{H2134} as crystal{H306}, going forth{H3318} from the throne{H3678} of YHWH{H3068} and the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נַחַל (nachal, H5158 — 'wadi/torrent-stream') — a seasonal watercourse carved into rock, fed by rain or springs (Gen 26:19, Deut 2:13, Ps 110:7). Greek has ποταμόν ('river' — a permanent, major waterway). A back-translator from Greek would use נָהָר (nahar — 'river'), not nachal. The wadi is a distinctly Semitic landscape feature; the Greek translator upgraded it to a river.

Uses מַיִם חַיִּים (mayim chayyim — 'living waters') — the Hebrew idiom for flowing spring water (Gen 26:19, Jer 2:13, 17:13, Zech 14:8). Greek has ὕδατος ζωῆς ('water of life'). 'Living waters' in Hebrew means water that MOVES (as opposed to stagnant cistern water); 'water of life' in Greek means water that grants eternal life. A back-translator from Greek would write מֵי הַחַיִּים ('waters of THE life'), not the idiomatic mayim chayyim.

Uses כְּאַחְלָמָה (ke-achlamah, H306 — 'like crystal/amethyst') — a High Priest breastplate stone from Exodus 28:19 and 39:12. Greek has ὡς κρύσταλλον ('like crystal'). A back-translator from Greek would write כבדולח or כקרח ('like ice/crystal'), not the Torah's priestly gemstone vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: nachal ('wadi'). Greek: ποταμόν ('river'). Different watercourse entirely.
Hebrew: 'full of living waters' (מלא ממים חיים). Greek: 'pure/clean water of life' (καθαρὸν ὕδατος ζωῆς). Hebrew emphasizes abundance and flow; Greek emphasizes purity and eternal life.
Hebrew: 'like achlamah' (breastplate stone). Greek: 'like crystal' (κρύσταλλον). Different comparison.
translation_notes: 'Wadi' for nachal preserves the specific Semitic landscape term — a torrent that flows through a rocky channel, often seasonal but here perpetually fed from the throne.
'Living waters' for mayim chayyim is the standard English rendering of this Hebrew idiom. See Jeremiah 2:13 where YHWH calls himself 'the fountain of living waters' (מְקוֹר מַיִם חַיִּים).
textual_notes: Zechariah 14:8 — 'And on that day living waters (מַיִם חַיִּים) shall go out from Yerushalayim.' The Hebrew Revelation preserves the prophetic idiom verbatim.
Ezekiel 47:1-12 describes water flowing from the threshold of the Temple eastward. The Hebrew nachal in Revelation connects to the nachal in Ezekiel's vision.

verses.translation: In the midst{H8432} of the plazas{H7339}, and upon the wadi{H5158}, there shall rise{H5927} upon its bank{H8193} from this side and from that, every{H3605} tree{H6086} of food{H3978} and the tree{H6086} of life{H2416}; and upon it were twelve{H8147}{H6240} kinds{H4327} of fruits{H6529}, and its fruit{H6529} was for food{H3978} and its leaf{H5929} for healing{H8644}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Ezekiel 47:12: וְעַל הַנַּחַל יַעֲלֶה עַל שְׂפָתוֹ מִזֶּה וּמִזֶּה כָּל עֵץ מַאֲכָל... וְהָיָה פִרְיוֹ לְמַאֲכָל וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה. The Hebrew preserves Ezekiel's exact phrasing word for word — nachal, ya'aleh, sefato, mizzeh umizzeh, kol ets ma'achal, piryo lema'achal, alehu litrupah. Greek Revelation completely restructures this: ξύλον ζωῆς ποιοῦν καρποὺς δώδεκα ('tree of life bearing twelve fruits'). A back-translator from Greek would NEVER reconstruct Ezekiel 47:12 verbatim.

CRITICAL: Hebrew has BOTH כָּל עֵץ מַאֲכָל ('every tree of food') AND עֵץ הַחַיִּים ('the tree of life'). Greek has ONLY ξύλον ζωῆς ('tree of life'). The Hebrew merges Ezekiel's 'every food tree' with Genesis 2:9's 'tree of life' — two OT streams flowing together. A back-translator from Greek, which has only 'tree of life,' would never add 'every tree of food.'
Uses רְחוֹבוֹת (rechovot — 'plazas/broad places', H7339, PLURAL). Greek has τῆς πλατείας (singular 'street'). Same plural usage as 21:21.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: Ezekiel 47:12 verbatim with the tree of life added. Greek: restructured into its own syntax.
Hebrew: 'every tree of food AND the tree of life.' Greek: only 'tree of life.' Hebrew has both; Greek dropped the Ezekiel food-trees.
Greek adds κατὰ μῆνα ἕνα ἕκαστον ἀποδιδοῦν τὸν καρπὸν αὐτοῦ ('each month yielding its fruit') — the monthly cycle detail absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'its leaf for healing' (singular leaf, unqualified). Greek: τὰ φύλλα τοῦ ξύλου εἰς θεραπείαν τῶν ἐθνῶν ('the leaves of the tree for healing of the nations'). Greek adds 'of the nations.'
translation_notes: 'Bank' for sefat (H8193 — literally 'lip') — the standard Hebrew word for a riverbank (Gen 41:3, Ex 2:3, Ezek 47:7).
תְּרוּפָה (terupah, H8644 — 'healing/medicine') from the root רפא (to heal). This word occurs in Ezekiel 47:12 and nowhere else in the OT — its appearance here confirms the direct Ezekiel quotation.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 47:12 (source text): וְעַל הַנַּחַל יַעֲלֶה עַל שְׂפָתוֹ מִזֶּה וּמִזֶּה כָּל עֵץ מַאֲכָל לֹא יִבּוֹל עָלֵהוּ וְלֹא יִתֹּם פִּרְיוֹ לָחֳדָשָׁיו יְבַכֵּר כִּי מֵימָיו מִן הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הֵמָּה יוֹצְאִים וְהָיָה פִרְיוֹ לְמַאֲכָל וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה. The Hebrew Revelation quotes the beginning and ending of this verse nearly verbatim, inserting 'the tree of life' from Genesis 2:9.

Genesis 2:9 — 'And YHWH Elohim caused to grow every tree pleasant to sight and good for food, and the tree of life (עֵץ הַחַיִּים) in the midst of the garden.' The Hebrew author sees the New Jerusalem as Eden restored, merging Genesis 2 with Ezekiel 47.

verses.translation: And the ban{H2764} shall not be{H1961} anymore{H5750}, and the throne{H3678} of YHWH{H3068} and the lamb{H7716} shall tabernacle{H7931} in her, and his servants{H5650} shall minister{H8334} to him.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֵרֶם (cherem, H2764 — 'the ban/devoted destruction'). This is the specific Torah term for total consecrated destruction — the annihilation of Jericho (Josh 6:17-18), the punishment for Achan's theft (Josh 7:1,11-12), the destruction of the Canaanites (Deut 7:2, 20:17). Greek has κατάθεμα ('curse'). A back-translator from Greek would use קְלָלָה (qelalah — 'curse') or אָלָה (alah — 'oath-curse'), NOT the weighty Torah concept of cherem. The Hebrew declares that the sacred ban — the mechanism of total destruction under YHWH's wrath — shall cease to exist.

Uses יִשְׁכּוֹן (yishkon, H7931 — 'shall dwell/tabernacle'), from the root שכן (shakan) — the root of שְׁכִינָה (Shekinah, the divine presence). Greek has ἔσται ('shall be'). The Hebrew says the throne TABERNACLES there — the Shekinah glory dwells. A back-translator from Greek would write יהיה ('shall be'), not the theologically loaded yishkon.

Uses יְשָׁרְתוּהוּ (yeshartuhu — 'shall minister to him', H8334) — the specific verb for Levitical/priestly ministry (Ex 28:35, Num 3:6, 1 Sam 2:11, Ezek 44:11). Greek has λατρεύσουσιν ('shall serve/worship'). The Hebrew specifies priestly liturgical service; the Greek uses generic worship. A back-translator from Greek would use יעבדו (ya'avdu — 'serve') or ישתחוו (yishtachavu — 'bow down'), not the priestly ministry verb sharat.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חרם ('the ban/devoted destruction'). Greek: κατάθεμα ('curse'). Entirely different concepts — sacred total destruction vs. a pronouncement of curse.
Hebrew: 'shall tabernacle' (ישכון — Shekinah root). Greek: 'shall be' (ἔσται). The Hebrew adds the dwelling/tabernacle theology.
translation_notes: 'Ban' for cherem captures the Torah concept without the full phrase 'devoted to destruction.' The cherem is the most extreme form of YHWH's judgment — total, irrevocable destruction (cf. Zechariah 14:11 — 'there shall be no more cherem').
'Tabernacle' for yishkon makes the Shekinah connection explicit. The throne does not merely exist in the city — it dwells there as YHWH dwelt in the Tabernacle.
'Minister' for yeshartu distinguishes Levitical priestly service from generic worship or servitude.
textual_notes: Zechariah 14:11 — וְחֵרֶם לֹא יִהְיֶה עוֹד ('and the cherem shall not be anymore'). The Hebrew Revelation quotes Zechariah 14:11 verbatim. The Greek translator paraphrased this as 'no more curse' (κατάθεμα), losing the Zechariah source.

verses.translation: And they shall see{H7200} his face{H6440}, and his name{H8034} shall be written{H3789} upon their foreheads{H4696}.

translation_notes: The promise 'they shall see his face' reverses Exodus 33:20 — 'You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live.' In the renewed creation, the barrier is removed.
מִצְחֵיהֶם (mitscheihem — 'their foreheads', H4696) — the same word used in Ezekiel 9:4 where the righteous are marked on the forehead (מֵצַח) for preservation.
textual_notes: Psalm 17:15 — 'As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when I awake with your likeness.' The face-to-face vision of God is the ultimate hope of the Psalms.

verses.translation: And the sun{H8121} shall not be{H1961} anymore{H5750} in her for light{H216} by day{H3119}, nor for brightness{H5051} shall the moon{H3394} give light{H215} to you; but YHWH{H3068} shall be to you for an everlasting{H5769} light{H216}, and your Elohim{H430} for your splendor{H8597}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 60:19: לֹא־יִהְיֶה־לָּךְ עוֹד הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לְאוֹר יוֹמָם וּלְנֹגַהּ הַיָּרֵחַ לֹא־יָאִיר לָךְ וְהָיָה־לָךְ יְהוָה לְאוֹר עוֹלָם וֵאלֹהַיִךְ לְתִפְאַרְתֵּךְ. The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Isaiah 60:19 WORD FOR WORD, including: (1) the 2nd person address לָךְ ('to you'), (2) the specific word נֹגַהּ ('brightness', H5051), (3) the divine name YHWH, (4) אוֹר עוֹלָם ('everlasting light'), and (5) the final phrase וֵאלֹהַיִךְ לְתִפְאַרְתֵּךְ ('and your Elohim for your splendor'). Greek Revelation 22:5 says: καὶ νὺξ οὐκ ἔσται ἐκεῖ, καὶ χρείαν οὐκ ἔχουσιν λύχνου καὶ φωτὸς ἡλίου, ὅτι κύριος ὁ θεὸς φωτιεῖ αὐτούς ('and night shall not be there, and they have no need of lamp nor light of sun, for the Lord God will illuminate them'). The Greek is a COMPLETE REPHRASING — 3rd person, no Isaiah vocabulary, no נגה, no תפארת, no direct quotation whatsoever. This is among the single strongest one-way markers in all of Revelation.

The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's 2nd person feminine singular address (לָךְ, אלהיִךְ, תפארתֵּךְ) — speaking directly to Jerusalem. Greek uses 3rd person plural (αὐτούς — 'them'). A back-translator from Greek's 3rd person would NEVER switch to 2nd person feminine singular, let alone reproduce Isaiah 60:19 verbatim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: VERBATIM Isaiah 60:19 in 2nd person feminine singular. Greek: entirely restructured paraphrase in 3rd person plural.

Hebrew: 'the sun shall not be anymore for light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give light to you.' Greek: 'they have no need of lamp nor light of sun.' Greek drops the moon, adds 'lamp,' changes the syntax entirely.
Hebrew: 'and your Elohim for your splendor' (תפארתך). Greek: completely absent — no equivalent at all.
Greek adds 'and they shall reign forever and ever' (βασιλεύσουσιν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) — absent from the Hebrew.
translation_notes: Translated in 2nd person feminine singular to preserve the Isaiah quotation: 'to you,' 'your Elohim,' 'your splendor.' The city is addressed as a woman, consistent with Jerusalem-as-bride throughout.
'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) — the same word used for the High Priest's garments (Ex 28:2, 28:40) meaning beauty/glory/ornamental splendor. YHWH himself becomes the city's adornment.
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:19 (exact source): לֹא־יִהְיֶה־לָּךְ עוֹד הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לְאוֹר יוֹמָם וּלְנֹגַהּ הַיָּרֵחַ לֹא־יָאִיר לָךְ וְהָיָה־לָךְ יְהוָה לְאוֹר עוֹלָם וֵאלֹהַיִךְ לְתִפְאַרְתֵּךְ. Isaiah 60:20 continues: לֹא־יָבוֹא עוֹד שִׁמְשֵׁךְ וִירֵחֵךְ לֹא יֵאָסֵף כִּי יְהוָה יִהְיֶה־לָּךְ לְאוֹר עוֹלָם וְשָׁלְמוּ יְמֵי אֶבְלֵךְ ('Your sun shall not set anymore, and your moon shall not withdraw itself, for YHWH shall be to you an everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed'). The Hebrew Revelation quotes v19 verbatim; the concept of v20 (end of mourning) was fulfilled in 21:4.

This Isaiah 60:19 verbatim quote in a Hebrew text of Revelation is perhaps the most decisive evidence for Hebrew priority in the entire book. No back-translator from the Greek paraphrase could reconstruct the original Isaiah prophecy word for word.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to me: These{H428} words{H1697} are indeed{H2005} truth{H571}. And YHWH{H3068} of Hosts{H6635} sent{H7971} his messenger{H4397} to show{H7200} his servants{H5650} what shall come to pass{H1961} shortly{H7138}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tsevaot — 'YHWH of Hosts/Armies', H6635) — the specific compound divine name occurring 285 times in the OT prophets (Isa 1:9, 6:3; Jer 7:3; Hag 1:2; Zech 1:3; Mal 1:4). Greek has κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων τῶν προφητῶν ('the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהֵי רוּחוֹת הַנְּבִיאִים ('Lord God of the spirits of the prophets'), NOT the specific OT title YHWH Tsevaot. The Greek translator apparently could not render the military-host concept and substituted a phrase about prophetic spirits.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: אמת ('truth' — one word). Greek: πιστοὶ καὶ ἀληθινοί ('faithful and true' — two words). Hebrew is more concise.
Hebrew: 'YHWH of Hosts' (יהוה צבאות). Greek: 'the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets' (κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων τῶν προφητῶν). Completely different divine title.
textual_notes: The phrase YHWH Tsevaot is the signature title of the later prophets — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi use it extensively. Its appearance here anchors the text in the Hebrew prophetic tradition.

verses.translation: See{H7200}! I shall come{H935} swiftly{H4120}. And holy{H6918} is he who believes{H539} in the words{H1697} of the prophecy{H5016}, what is written{H3789} in this scroll{H5612}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קָדוֹשׁ (kadosh — 'holy', H6918). Greek has μακάριος ('blessed/happy'). These are fundamentally different concepts — kadosh means 'set apart, consecrated, belonging to YHWH' while makarios means 'fortunate, blessed, happy.' A back-translator from Greek would use אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei — 'happy/blessed'), NOT kadosh. The Hebrew author declares the believer HOLY, not merely happy.

Uses מַאֲמִין (ma'amin — 'believes/trusts', H539, from the root אמן — amen). Greek has τηρῶν ('keeps/guards'). Believing and keeping are different activities — one is internal faith, the other external observance. A back-translator from Greek would use שׁוֹמֵר (shomer — 'keeper/guardian'), not the faith-verb ma'amin.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: קדוש ('holy'). Greek: μακάριος ('blessed'). Different attribute entirely.
Hebrew: שמאמין ('who believes'). Greek: ὁ τηρῶν ('who keeps/guards'). Different activity.
translation_notes: The word [אָבֹא] appears in brackets in the source, indicating editorial restoration of a damaged or unclear reading. The consonantal text supports אבוא (from בוא — 'to come').
בִּמְהֵרָה (bimherah — 'swiftly/hastily', H4120) — from the root מהר (to hasten). This is the standard Hebrew word for 'quickly' in a theological context (Ps 31:3, 79:8, 143:7).

verses.translation: And I, Yochanan{H3110}, heard{H8085} and saw{H7200} all{H3605} these things. And when I heard{H8085} and saw{H7200} this, I fell{H5307} to the ground{H776} and prayed{H6419} to the messenger{H4397} who showed{H7200} me this.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וְהִתְפַּלַּלְתִּי (vehitpallalti — 'and I prayed', H6419, hitpa'el of פלל). Greek has προσκυνῆσαι ('to worship/prostrate'). הִתְפַּלֵּל is the reflexive verb specifically meaning 'to pray' — the standard Hebrew word for directing prayer (1 Kings 8:28, Dan 9:4, Neh 1:4). Greek προσκυνέω means 'to bow in worship.' A back-translator from Greek would write וָאֶשְׁתַּחֲוֶה (va-eshtachaveh — 'and I bowed in worship'), NOT the prayer verb hitpallel. The Hebrew says Yochanan PRAYED to the messenger; the Greek says he WORSHIPPED.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I prayed to the messenger' (התפללתי). Greek: 'I fell to worship before the feet of the messenger' (ἔπεσα προσκυνῆσαι ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ποδῶν). Different activity (prayer vs. worship) and Greek adds 'before the feet.'
Hebrew: 'I fell to the ground' (נפלתי לארץ). Greek: ἔπεσα ('I fell'). Hebrew specifies 'to the ground/earth.'
translation_notes: כֵּיוָן (keivan) — a later Hebrew conjunction meaning 'when/since.' Not a standard OT term; common in Mishnaic Hebrew.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to me: See{H7200}! Do not do{H6213} this, for I too am from your fellowship{H2270} and from the brothers{H251} the prophets{H5030}, and from those who uphold{H6965} the words{H1697} of this scroll{H5612}. Make{H6213} your prayer{H8605} to YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַבְרוּתְךָ (chavrutecha — 'your fellowship/companionship', from the root חבר H2270 — 'companion/fellow'). Greek has σύνδουλός σου ('your fellow-servant'). The Hebrew חברות (chavrut) is a distinctly Semitic concept — a study partnership, companionship of equals. A back-translator from Greek σύνδουλος would write עֶבֶד כָּמוֹךָ ('a servant like you'), not the fellowship-companion word.

Uses הַמְּקַיְּימִים (hamequyemim — 'those who uphold/establish', H6965, from קום in the hiphil — 'to cause to stand/establish'). Greek has τηρούντων ('those who keep/guard'). The Hebrew implies actively ESTABLISHING and UPHOLDING the words — making them stand firm — while the Greek implies passively GUARDING them. Different postures toward the text.

Uses עֲשֵׂי תְּפִלָּתְךָ לְיַהְוֶה ('make your prayer to YHWH', H8605). Greek has τῷ θεῷ προσκύνησον ('worship God'). Again prayer vs. worship, and YHWH vs. generic 'God.' The Hebrew-Greek prayer/worship distinction is CONSISTENT across vv. 8-9, suggesting a systematic difference in the author's understanding.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from your fellowship' (חברותך — fellowship of equals). Greek: 'your fellow-servant' (σύνδουλος — shared servitude). Different relational concept.
Hebrew: 'Make your prayer to YHWH.' Greek: 'Worship God.' Prayer vs. worship; YHWH vs. θεός.
translation_notes: 'Fellowship' for chavrutecha — the root חבר means 'to join/be united' and the noun describes a bond of companionship. In later rabbinic literature, chavruta becomes the technical term for a Torah study partner.
'Uphold' for mequyemim — distinguishing the active establishment of the words from mere passive guarding.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to me: Do not seal{H5640} the vision{H2377} of this scroll{H5612}, for the time{H6256} is near{H7138}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הֶחָזוֹן (hachazon — 'the vision', H2377). Greek has τοὺς λόγους τῆς προφητείας ('the words of the prophecy'). חָזוֹן is the specific prophetic-vision word — the opening word of Isaiah (חֲזוֹן יְשַׁעְיָהוּ, Isa 1:1), used for Daniel's sealed visions (Dan 8:26, 12:4). A back-translator from Greek 'words of the prophecy' would write דִּבְרֵי הַנְּבוּאָה, not chazon.

Uses תִּסְתֹּם (tistom — 'seal/stop up', H5640, from סתם). This is the EXACT verb from Daniel 8:26 — סְתֹם הֶחָזוֹן ('seal the vision') and Daniel 12:4 — סְתֹם הַדְּבָרִים ('seal the words'). The Hebrew Revelation deliberately REVERSES Daniel's command: Daniel was told TO seal; Yochanan is told NOT to seal. A back-translator from Greek σφραγίσῃς ('seal') could also use חתם (chatam), but the specific use of סתם ties this to Daniel's Hebrew, not to a Greek source.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the vision' (החזון — the prophetic vision). Greek: 'the words of the prophecy' (τοὺς λόγους τῆς προφητείας). Different object being left unsealed.
translation_notes: 'Vision' for chazon preserves the technical prophetic term — this is not generic 'words' but a seen revelation.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:26 — סְתֹם הֶחָזוֹן כִּי לְיָמִים רַבִּים ('seal the vision, for it is for many days'). Daniel 12:4 — סְתֹם הַדְּבָרִים וַחֲתֹם הַסֵּפֶר עַד עֵת קֵץ ('seal the words and close the scroll until the time of the end'). The Hebrew Revelation inverts Daniel: DO NOT seal, for the time is NEAR — not far off.

verses.translation: Whoever has evil{H7451}, let him be so for all time{H6256}; whoever has uncleanness{H2931}, let him likewise be so; but whoever is pious{H2623}, let him be so for all time{H6256}; and whoever is holy{H6918}, likewise so.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חָסִיד (chasid — 'pious one', H2623) — the specific Hebrew term for one characterized by חֶסֶד (chesed — covenant loyalty/faithful love). Greek has δίκαιος ('righteous/just'). These are NOT the same concept: a chasid is defined by loyal love and covenant faithfulness; a dikaios is defined by justice and legal righteousness. A back-translator from Greek would use צַדִּיק (tsaddiq — 'righteous'), the standard Hebrew equivalent of δίκαιος, NOT chasid. The chasid is a uniquely Hebrew concept with no Greek equivalent.

Uses טָמֵא (tamei — 'unclean', H2931) — the specific Levitical purity term for ritual impurity (Lev 11-15, Num 19). Greek has ῥυπαρός ('filthy' — moral dirtiness). A back-translator from Greek would use מְלוּכְלָךְ or מְזוּהָם ('dirty/soiled'), not the priestly-ritual purity word tamei. The Hebrew frames the contrast in Levitical categories: clean/unclean (tahor/tamei), holy/profane.
Uses כָּל עֵת ('all time' — forever/perpetually). Greek has ἔτι ('still/yet'). The Hebrew declares a permanent, eternal state; the Greek suggests ongoing continuation. Different temporal scope.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: רע ('evil' — moral character). Greek: ὁ ἀδικῶν ('the unjust one' — one doing wrong). Character vs. action.
Hebrew: טמא ('unclean' — Levitical impurity). Greek: ῥυπαρός ('filthy' — moral dirt). Different conceptual framework.
Hebrew: חסיד ('pious' — covenant loyalty). Greek: δίκαιος ('righteous/just'). Different virtue.
Hebrew: כל עת ('all time' — permanent). Greek: ἔτι ('still/yet' — continuing).
translation_notes: 'Pious' for chasid — capturing the chesed/loyal-love dimension. The chasid in the Psalms is YHWH's faithful one (Ps 4:4, 12:2, 16:10, 32:6, 86:2, 149:1,5). It is the root of Hasidim — the 'pious ones.'
textual_notes: The four-fold contrast (evil/unclean vs. pious/holy) maps onto Levitical categories, not Greek ethical ones. The Hebrew author thinks in terms of purity and holiness (tahor/tamei, kadosh/chol), not in terms of Greek justice and moral virtue.

verses.translation: And see{H7200}! I shall come{H935} swiftly{H4120}, to repay{H7999} every{H3605} man{H376} according to his deed{H4639}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לְשַׁלֵּם (leshalem — 'to repay/recompense', H7999, from the root שלם — shalom/completeness). The Hebrew verb carries the connotation of making complete, restoring wholeness, fulfilling an obligation. Greek has ἀποδοῦναι ('to give back/render'). The Hebrew root connects repayment to SHALOM — the restoration of cosmic balance. A back-translator from Greek would use להשיב (lehashiv — 'to return/restore'), not the shalom-rooted leshalem.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὁ μισθός μου μετ' ἐμοῦ ('my reward is with me') — absent from the Hebrew. This phrase echoes Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 in the Greek tradition, but the Hebrew text here does not include it.
Hebrew: כמעשהו ('according to his deed' — singular). Greek: ὡς τὸ ἔργον αὐτοῦ ἔσται ('as his work shall be'). Hebrew refers to the completed deed; Greek to the work that shall be.
translation_notes: The word [אָבֹא] again appears in brackets in the source, as in v7.
'Repay' for leshalem captures the completion/wholeness nuance of the shalom root.
textual_notes: Psalm 62:13 — 'For you repay (תְשַׁלֵּם) to a man according to his deed (כְּמַעֲשֵׂהוּ).' The Hebrew Revelation uses the exact Psalm 62 phrasing. The Greek paraphrases differently.

verses.translation: I am the first{H7223} and the last{H314}, the beginning and the end{H5490}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן ('the first and the last') — a DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 where YHWH declares: 'I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god.' Greek has τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος ('the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last'). If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would write הָאָלֶף וְהַתָּו ('the Aleph and the Tav') for Alpha and Omega. Instead, the Hebrew preserves Isaiah's self-declaration of YHWH. The Greek translator converted the Hebrew theological concept to Greek letters and expanded two titles to three. This is the same decisive one-way marker seen in 21:6.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: TWO titles — 'the first and the last' + 'the beginning and the end.' Greek: THREE titles — adds 'the Alpha and the Omega.' Hebrew never mentions Greek letters.
Hebrew order: first/last, then beginning/end. Greek order: Alpha/Omega, beginning/end, first/last. Different sequence.
translation_notes: תְּחִילַּת (techilat — 'beginning') is a later Hebrew form from the root חלל. It lacks a standard Strong's number but is common in Mishnaic Hebrew.
textual_notes: Isaiah 44:6 — כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגֹאֲלוֹ יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן וַאֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן וּמִבַּלְעָדַי אֵין אֱלֹהִים ('Thus says YHWH, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, YHWH of Hosts: I am the first and I am the last; and besides me there is no god'). Isaiah 48:12 — אֲנִי הוּא אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן אַף אֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן ('I am he; I am the first, indeed I am the last'). The speaker claims YHWH's exclusive self-identification from Isaiah.

verses.translation: Holy{H6918} are they who do{H6213} his commandments{H4687}, so that they shall have a portion{H2506} in the tree{H6086} of life{H2416} and merit{H2135} to go forth from the city{H5892}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קְדוֹשִׁים (kedoshim — 'holy ones', H6918). Greek has μακάριοι ('blessed/happy'). Same kadosh vs. makarios distinction as v7. The Hebrew frames commandment-keeping as a matter of holiness; the Greek frames it as a matter of blessedness.

Uses מִצְוֹתָיו (mitsvotav — 'his commandments', H4687) — the standard Torah term for divine commands (Ex 20:6, Deut 5:10, 6:2, 8:1). Greek also has ἐντολάς ('commandments'). Both traditions agree here.

Uses חֵלֶק (cheleq — 'portion/allotment', H2506) — the word for a tribal inheritance (Josh 19:9, Deut 10:9 — 'YHWH is their cheleq'). Greek has ἐξουσία ('authority/right'). A back-translator from Greek would use רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'permission/authority'), not the land-inheritance word cheleq. The Hebrew frames access to the tree of life as a COVENANT INHERITANCE, like a tribal allotment in the Promised Land.

Uses מֵהָעִיר ('from the city'). Greek has εἰσέλθωσιν εἰς τὴν πόλιν ('enter INTO the city'). OPPOSITE direction — the Hebrew says 'from/out of the city,' the Greek says 'into the city.' The Hebrew envisions the righteous as citizens of the city who go forth from it freely, while v15's outsiders cannot enter. The Greek envisions the righteous entering a city they are outside of.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: קדושים ('holy'). Greek: μακάριοι ('blessed'). Same deviation as v7.
Hebrew: חלק ('portion' — inheritance). Greek: ἐξουσία ('authority/right'). Different concept.
Hebrew: לילך מהעיר ('to go forth FROM the city'). Greek: εἰσέλθωσιν εἰς τὴν πόλιν ('enter INTO the city'). Opposite direction of movement.
translation_notes: 'Commandments' for mitsvotav — the Torah's specific term for divine commands, not generic moral precepts.
'Portion' for cheleq preserves the covenant-inheritance concept.

'Merit' for yizkeh (H2135, from זכה — 'to be clean/pure' → 'to merit/be worthy') — a word that develops its 'merit' meaning in later Hebrew. The idea is that keeping commandments PURIFIES one to be worthy.
textual_notes: Genesis 3:22-24 — man is expelled FROM the garden and barred from the tree of life. The Hebrew Revelation reverses this: the commandment-keepers regain their portion in the tree of life and their right to go forth from the city-garden. The direction 'from the city' may echo the Edenic going-forth.

verses.translation: For outside{H2351} stand{H5975} the dogs{H3611} and the sorcerers{H3784} and the harlots{H2181} and the murderers{H7523} and the liars.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִבַּחוּץ עוֹמְדִים ('from outside, standing', H5975). Greek has only ἔξω ('outside'). The Hebrew adds the verb עמד ('to stand') — they are POSITIONED and STANDING outside, a concrete image of exclusion. This verbal specificity is characteristic of Hebrew narrative, not translation from Greek.

Uses הַזּוֹנוֹת (hazzonot — 'the harlots', H2181, FEMININE PLURAL). Greek has πόρνοι ('fornicators', MASCULINE). The Hebrew specifically means female harlots — women who sell sexual services. The Greek means male sexual sinners. A back-translator from Greek's masculine πόρνοι would use זוֹנִים (zonim — masculine) or מְנָאֲפִים (mena'afim — 'adulterers'), not the feminine זונות.

Uses כְּלָבִים (kelavim — 'dogs', H3611) — in Hebrew a term of profound contempt for the ritually impure and the spiritually worthless (1 Sam 17:43, 2 Sam 3:8, 2 Kings 8:13). In Deut 23:19 'dog' (כלב) is a term for a male cult prostitute. The Hebrew resonance is far richer than the Greek κύνες.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 5 categories (dogs, sorcerers, harlots, murderers, liars). Greek: 6 categories (dogs, sorcerers, fornicators, murderers, idolaters, liars). Greek adds εἰδωλολάτραι ('idolaters') which is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: הזונות (feminine harlots). Greek: πόρνοι (masculine fornicators). Different gender and shade of meaning.
Greek: πᾶς ὁ φιλῶν καὶ ποιῶν ψεῦδος ('everyone loving and practicing a lie'). Hebrew: הכזבנים ('the liars'). Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: כַּזְבָנִים (kazbanim — 'liars') is a later Hebrew agentive form from כזב (kazav — to lie). No standard Strong's number. Same form as in 21:8.
רַצְחָנִים (ratshanim — 'murderers') is a late Hebrew agentive from רצח (ratsach, H7523 — 'to murder'). The -an/-anim suffix is characteristic of Mishnaic Hebrew.

verses.translation: I, Yeshua, have sent{H7971} my messenger{H4397} to show{H7200} to the congregation{H5712}. And I am the root{H8328} from the families{H4940} of David{H1732}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵדָה (edah — 'congregation', H5712) — the specific OT term for the assembled congregation of Israel (Num 1:2, 16:3, 27:17, Josh 22:16). Greek has ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('the churches' — plural). A back-translator from Greek would use קְהִלּוֹת (kehilot — 'assemblies') or transliterate ἐκκλησία. The Hebrew author uses the singular edah — THE congregation, as a unified body — not plural 'churches.' This reflects an Israelite assembly theology, not a diaspora church structure.

Uses שֹׁרֶשׁ מִמִּשְׁפְּחוֹת דָּוִד ('the root FROM the families of David'). Greek has ἡ ῥίζα καὶ τὸ γένος τοῦ Δαυΐδ ('the root AND the offspring of David'). The Hebrew says the root comes FROM David's families — a claim of Davidic origin. The Greek says he is BOTH root (source) AND offspring (descendant) — a theological paradox absent from the Hebrew. A back-translator from Greek would include 'and the offspring' (וְצֶאֱצָא), not the simple directional 'from the families.'

Greek adds ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς ὁ πρωϊνός ('the bright morning star') — completely ABSENT from the Hebrew. This is one of the most recognizable phrases in Greek Revelation, and it is simply not in the Hebrew text.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: להראות לעדה ('to show to the congregation'). Greek: μαρτυρῆσαι ὑμῖν ταῦτα ἐπὶ ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('to testify to you these things for the churches'). 'Show' vs. 'testify'; singular 'congregation' vs. plural 'churches.'
Hebrew: 'the root from the families of David.' Greek: 'the root and the offspring of David.' Different claim.
Greek adds 'the bright morning star' — absent from Hebrew entirely.
translation_notes: 'Root' for shoresh (H8328) — Isaiah 11:10 uses the same word: 'the root of Jesse' (שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשַׁי). The claim is Davidic/Messianic.
'Congregation' for edah preserves the OT assembly concept without importing 'church' from the Greek.
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:1,10 — 'A shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots (שָׁרָשָׁיו) shall bear fruit... On that day the root of Jesse (שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשַׁי) shall stand as a signal for the peoples.' The shoresh/root claim is deeply Isaianic.

verses.translation: And the spirit{H7307} and the bride{H3618} say{H559}: Come{H935}! And whoever hears{H8085}, let him say{H559}: Come{H935}! And whoever is thirsty{H6771}, go{H1980} to living{H2416} waters{H4325} and drink{H8354}, without{H3808} silver{H3701} and without price{H4242}.

one_way_hebrew: NEAR-VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 55:1: הוֹי כָּל צָמֵא לְכוּ לַמַּיִם... בְּלוֹא כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר ('Ho, all who thirst, go to the waters... without silver and without price'). The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact phrasing: the plural imperative לְכוּ ('go!'), the compound negation בְּלוֹא כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר ('without silver and without price'), and the specific word כֶסֶף ('silver' — not generic 'money'). Greek changes everything: ἐρχέσθω ('let him come' — singular, different verb), λαβέτω ὕδωρ ζωῆς δωρεάν ('let him take the water of life freely' — one word δωρεάν replaces the whole Isaiah phrase). A back-translator from Greek would NEVER reconstruct the full Isaiah 55:1 quotation.

Uses מַיִם חַיִּים (mayim chayyim — 'living waters') again, as in v1. Greek has ὕδωρ ζωῆς ('water of life'). The consistent Hebrew use of 'living waters' (flowing spring water) versus Greek 'water of life' (life-granting water) shows a systematic Hebrew idiom that a translator would not maintain.
Uses the plural imperatives לְכוּ... וּשְׁתוּ ('go ye... and drink ye') — addressing the thirsty masses. Greek uses singular. The Hebrew preserves Isaiah 55:1's plural address to the crowds.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: full Isaiah 55:1 quotation — 'go to living waters and drink without silver and without price.' Greek: 'let him come... let him take the water of life freely.' The Hebrew quotes Isaiah; the Greek paraphrases.
Hebrew: 'living waters' (mayim chayyim — flowing water). Greek: 'water of life' (ὕδωρ ζωῆς — life-granting water). Same systematic divergence as v1.
Hebrew: plural imperatives (לכו, שתו). Greek: singular (ἐρχέσθω, λαβέτω).
Hebrew: בלוא כסף ובלוא מחיר ('without silver and without price' — two-part negation). Greek: δωρεάν ('freely' — one word).
translation_notes: 'Bride' for kalah (H3618) — the standard Hebrew word for bride. This is the bride from 21:2,9.
'Silver' for kesef (H3701) — Hebrew uses 'silver' where English says 'money.' Kesef is both the metal and the currency.
'Price' for mechir (H4242) — the cost or payment for goods (2 Sam 24:24, 1 Kings 10:28, Lam 5:4).
textual_notes: Isaiah 55:1 (source text): הוֹי כָּל צָמֵא לְכוּ לַמַּיִם וַאֲשֶׁר אֵין לוֹ כָּסֶף לְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ וְאִכְלוּ וּלְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ בְּלוֹא כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר יַיִן וְחָלָב. The Hebrew Revelation condenses Isaiah's invitation but preserves the key phrases verbatim: the thirsty, go to waters, without silver, without price.

verses.translation: But I testify{H5749} to all{H3605} who hear{H8085} the prophecy{H5016} of this scroll{H5612}: and if one{H259} should add{H3254} to it any words{H1697}, YHWH{H3068} shall add{H3254} upon him the plagues{H5061} that are written{H3789} in this scroll{H5612}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the verb pair יוֹסִיף... יוֹסִיף (yosif... yosif — 'add... add', H3254) — a Hebrew word-play: if one ADDS to the scroll, YHWH will ADD plagues. This measure-for-measure (middah keneged middah) literary device is characteristic of Hebrew rhetoric and Torah law. Greek also uses the same verb (ἐπιθῇ... ἐπιθήσει) but the literary weight of the Hebrew word-play is native to the Semitic text.

Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues', H5061) — the same Levitical plague-word as in 21:9 (plagues of Egypt, Ex 11:1; priestly skin plagues, Lev 13-14). Greek has πληγάς ('blows/plagues' — generic). The Levitical term is consistent throughout the Hebrew text.
Uses יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) as the agent who adds plagues. Greek has ὁ θεός ('God'). The Hebrew preserves the Tetragrammaton; the Greek substitutes a generic title.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: יהוה ('YHWH'). Greek: ὁ θεός ('God').
translation_notes: מֵעִיד (me'id — 'testifying/bearing witness', H5749) — from the root עוד (to testify). This is formal legal testimony, not casual assertion.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 4:2 — לֹא תֹסִפוּ עַל הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה אֶתְכֶם וְלֹא תִגְרְעוּ מִמֶּנּוּ ('You shall not ADD to the word that I command you, and you shall not DIMINISH from it'). Deuteronomy 12:32 repeats: לֹא תֹסֵף עָלָיו וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ. Verses 18-19 together reproduce the Deuteronomic prohibition using the EXACT same Hebrew verb pair: יוסיף (add, H3254) in v18, יגרע (diminish, H1639) in v19.

verses.translation: And if one{H259} should diminish{H1639} any words{H1697} from this scroll{H5612}, YHWH{H3068} shall blot out{H4229} his name{H8034} from the scroll{H5612} of life{H2416}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יִמְחֶה... שְׁמוֹ מִסֵּפֶר הַחַיִּים ('shall blot out his NAME from the scroll of life', H4229). Greek has ἀφελεῖ ὁ θεὸς τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ βίβλου τῆς ζωῆς ('God shall take away his PORTION from the book of life'). The Hebrew uses the verb מָחָה (machah — 'to blot out/wipe away') — the EXACT verb from Exodus 32:33 where YHWH says: מִי אֲשֶׁר חָטָא לִי אֶמְחֶנּוּ מִסִּפְרִי ('whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book'). And it is a NAME that is blotted — matching Deuteronomy 9:14 and 29:19. A back-translator from Greek's 'take away his portion' would use יסיר חלקו ('remove his share'), NOT the Exodus/Deuteronomy machah-from-the-book language.

Uses יִגְרַע (yigra — 'shall diminish', H1639) — the EXACT counterpart to יוסיף ('add', H3254) in v18. Together they reproduce the Deuteronomy 4:2 pair: תוסיפו / תגרעו ('add / diminish'). This verb pair is a Torah legal formula. The Greek uses different verbs (ἐπιθῇ / ἀφαιρῇ) that do not carry the Torah resonance.

Uses מִסֵּפֶר הַחַיִּים (mi-sefer hachayyim — 'from the scroll of life'). This is the OT concept from Psalm 69:29: יִמָּחוּ מִסֵּפֶר חַיִּים ('let them be blotted out from the scroll of the living'). Same verb (machah), same phrase (sefer chayyim). The Hebrew Revelation quotes the Psalms.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall blot out his NAME' (ימחה שמו — Exodus 32:33 language). Greek: 'shall take away his PORTION' (ἀφελεῖ τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ). Different object — name vs. portion.
Hebrew: ימחה ('blot out' — the wiping/erasing verb). Greek: ἀφελεῖ ('take away' — the removing verb). Different action.

Greek adds: 'and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book' (καὶ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως τῆς ἁγίας, καὶ τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν βιβλίῳ τούτῳ) — expanded consequences absent from the more concise Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Blot out' for yimcheh — the verb of erasure. In ancient scrolls, text was physically wiped/scraped away. The image is YHWH personally erasing the person's name from the registered living.
'Scroll of life' for sefer hachayyim — a registry of the living, not a 'book' in the modern sense. See Psalm 69:29, Daniel 12:1, Exodus 32:32-33.
textual_notes: Exodus 32:32-33 — Moses says: 'blot me out (מְחֵנִי) from your scroll (מִסִּפְרְךָ).' YHWH replies: 'Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out (אֶמְחֶנּוּ) from my scroll.' The Hebrew Revelation uses this same Mosaic vocabulary for the ultimate threat against those who corrupt Scripture.

verses.translation: And thus{H3541} said{H559} the one who testifies{H5749} this: Yes{H3651}, I shall come{H935} swiftly{H4120}. Amen{H543}. Yes{H3651}, come{H935}, lord{H113} Yeshua!

one_way_hebrew: Uses וְכֹה אָמַר (vekhoh amar — 'and thus said', H3541) — the PROPHETIC FORMULA. כֹּה אָמַר ('thus says') introduces divine speech throughout the prophets (Isa 7:7, 10:24, 28:16, 37:6; Jer 2:2, 4:3, 6:6; Ezek 2:4, 3:11, etc.). Greek has Λέγει ('he says' — present tense). A back-translator from Greek would write אוֹמֵר ('says'), not the formulaic prophetic koh amar.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: וכה אמר ('and thus said' — prophetic formula, past tense). Greek: Λέγει ('says' — present tense).
translation_notes: 'Lord' for adon (H113) — the human/relational title of authority, not the divine name. Calling Yeshua 'adon' parallels how subjects address their king (1 Sam 22:12, 2 Sam 14:9).

verses.translation: The lovingkindness{H2617} from our lord{H113} Yeshua the Anointed{H4899} shall be{H1961} with all{H3605} of you. Amen{H543}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֶסֶד (chesed — 'lovingkindness/covenant loyalty', H2617). Greek has χάρις (charis — 'grace'). These are NOT equivalent concepts. Chesed is YHWH's faithful love bound by covenant — the quality that drives his loyalty to Israel despite their failures (Ex 34:6-7, Ps 136, Mic 7:18-20). Charis is unmerited favor — a gift given without obligation. A back-translator from Greek χάρις would use חֵן (chen — 'grace/favor', H2580), the standard Hebrew equivalent, NOT chesed. The closing benediction of the Hebrew Revelation invokes covenant loyalty, not free grace — a fundamentally different theological framework.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חסד ('lovingkindness/covenant loyalty'). Greek: χάρις ('grace'). Different theological concept for the closing benediction.
translation_notes: 'Lovingkindness' for chesed — no single English word captures this concept. It combines loyalty, love, faithfulness, and covenant obligation. Alternatives: 'loyal love,' 'covenant faithfulness,' 'steadfast love.'
'Anointed' for mashiach (H4899) — the Hebrew word Messiah, meaning 'one anointed with oil.' Greek Χριστός ('Christ') is a translation of this Hebrew term.
textual_notes: Psalm 136 uses חסד 26 times: כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ ('for his chesed endures forever'). The closing of the Hebrew Revelation invokes this same covenant quality — YHWH's enduring faithful love channeled through the Anointed One.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 22 in Hebrew is saturated with verbatim OT quotations and Torah-specific vocabulary that could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers. The most decisive are: (1) Verse 5 — VERBATIM Isaiah 60:19, word for word, including 2nd person feminine address (לָךְ, אלהיִךְ, תפארתֵּךְ), where the Greek is a complete 3rd-person rephrasing with zero Isaiah vocabulary. (2) Verse 2 — VERBATIM Ezekiel 47:12, preserving the prophet's exact syntax (ועל הנחל יעלה על שפתו מזה ומזה כל עץ מאכל... פריו למאכל ועלהו לתרופה), PLUS the insertion of Genesis 2:9's 'tree of life' — merging two OT streams. (3) Verse 17 — Isaiah 55:1 quotation (לכו למים חיים... בלוא כסף ובלוא מחיר). (4) Verse 13 — 'the first and the last' (Isaiah 44:6) instead of 'Alpha and Omega.' (5) Verse 3 — חרם (cherem, the sacred ban — Zechariah 14:11 verbatim) instead of 'curse.' (6) Verses 18-19 — the יוסיף/יגרע (add/diminish) verb pair from Deuteronomy 4:2, with verse 19 using Exodus 32:33's מחה (blot out) language. (7) Verse 21 — חסד (covenant loyalty) closing the book instead of χάρις (grace). The systematic differences — prayer vs. worship (vv. 8-9), holy vs. blessed (vv. 7, 14), pious vs. righteous (v. 11), living waters vs. water of life (vv. 1, 17), YHWH of Hosts vs. 'God of the spirits of the prophets' (v. 6), edah vs. churches (v. 16), cherem vs. curse (v. 3), and the blotting-out of the NAME vs. removal of a PORTION (v. 19) — reveal two texts with fundamentally different theological vocabularies. The Hebrew thinks in Levitical categories (tamei/kadosh, chasid, cherem, nega'im, sharat), quotes the prophets verbatim, and uses priestly terminology throughout. The Greek operates with its own conceptual framework. The direction of dependence is clear: the Hebrew is the source.
